summary: Describes sending syslog messages over Datagram TLS (DTLS). It gives a secure way to carry log messages when a connectionless transport is wanted.

plainLanguage.summary: Computers send diary notes called logs to a central place. This keeps those notes secret and tamper-proof, even when they are sent as separate loose packets.

questions: which port does syslog over dtls use
can syslog over dtls use tcp
subtitle: How to carry syslog messages over DTLS on UDP or DCCP, with encryption, authentication and replay protection.

tldr.problem: Syslog needs a secure transport in cases where a connectionless transport is wanted, since syslog over TLS needs TCP.
tldr.mechanism: Each syslog message is sent as DTLS application data, framed with a decimal length prefix, over UDP (required) or DCCP (recommended where available), on port 6514.
tldr.outcome: Syslog gets confidentiality, integrity, authentication, cookie-based denial-of-service defence and replay protection hop by hop, but delivery is still unreliable and messages can be lost.

today: RFC 6012 is a Proposed Standard. It has been updated by RFC 8996 and RFC 9662, so check those for current requirements. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Syslog Meets DTLS
sections.content:
The syslog protocol (RFC 5424) is designed to run over different transports. This RFC defines how to carry it over Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS, RFC 4347), which is built for applications that need secure datagram transport. DTLS has been mapped onto UDP and onto the Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP), and this memo defines both options: syslog over DTLS over UDP and syslog over DTLS over DCCP.

The roles come from syslog: an originator generates content, a collector gathers it, and a relay forwards it. A transport sender is always the DTLS client and a transport receiver is always the DTLS server.
sections.plainLanguage: Syslog is how computers write down what happened. This is a way to send those notes in a locked, sealed envelope, one loose envelope at a time.

sections.title: Security Requirements and What DTLS Provides
sections.content:
The security requirements of RFC 5425 apply. One added threat is denial of service: an attacker may use a spoofed IP source to start a cryptographic handshake and burn the server's resources.

DTLS counters the primary threats with confidentiality, hop-by-hop integrity checking, and server or mutual authentication. It adds a cookie exchange during the handshake against denial of service and a sequence number in the header against replay.

This only secures transport hop by hop and is not concerned with message contents. The authenticated identity of the sender, such as a certificate subject name, is not necessarily related to the HOSTNAME field of the syslog message. When origin authentication is needed, RFC 5848 can be used.
sections.plainLanguage: The sealed envelope keeps the note private and shows if it was changed. A secret handshake word stops strangers from tying up the mail room, and numbered envelopes stop someone resending an old one.

sections.title: Transport, Ports and Starting a Session
sections.content:
Implementations MUST support DTLS over UDP and SHOULD support DTLS over DCCP. Syslog over DTLS over TCP MUST NOT be used; for TCP, use syslog over TLS (RFC 5425). Because UDP and DCCP give no session multiplexing, the implementer maps a unique combination of remote address, remote port, local address and local port to a session.

Port 6514 over UDP and DCCP is the default, and the DCCP service code SYLG (1398361159) was assigned to syslog.

The sender starts by sending a DTLS Client Hello. Implementations MUST support the DTLS denial of service countermeasures: the receiver answers with a Hello Verify Request containing a cookie, and the sender repeats its Client Hello with that cookie to begin the handshake. No syslog message may be sent before the handshake succeeds. Implementations MUST support DTLS 1.0 and the cipher suite TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA, and MUST NOT negotiate a suite with NULL integrity or authentication.

Where privacy is required, a non-NULL encryption algorithm must be negotiated or privacy achieved by other means such as a physically secured network. Where it is not, the RFC notes that a NULL encryption algorithm can help operations staff who sniff packets.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender knocks, the receiver replies with a ticket number, and the sender must show the ticket before any notes are accepted. That way, fake knockers cannot waste the receiver's time.

sections.title: Certificate-Based Authentication
sections.content:
Both sender and receiver MUST implement certificate-based authentication, which means validating the certificate and checking that the peer holds the matching private key (the latter done by DTLS). The validation methods in Sections 4.2.1 and 4.2.2 of RFC 5425 SHALL be implemented for interoperability.

Both sides MUST also be able to generate a key pair and self-signed certificate if none is available otherwise. They SHOULD provide ways to record the certificate or its fingerprint used by the remote endpoint, to link an identity to the data sent or received.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides show an ID card and prove it is really theirs. If someone has no ID card, they can make one, and the other side may write down what it looks like.

sections.title: Framing, Message Size and Closing
sections.content:
All syslog messages MUST be sent as DTLS application data. One DTLS record may hold several messages, or one message may span several records. Each frame is a decimal octet count, a single space, then the syslog message, as defined by the ABNF in the RFC.

The receiver MUST use that length to delimit messages. There is no upper limit per se, but a message SHOULD NOT exceed the DTLS maximum record size of 2^14 bytes. A receiver MUST process messages up to and including 2048 octets and SHOULD process up to and including 8192 octets.

To close, a sender MUST send a DTLS close_notify alert before closing, and need not wait for the receiver's. A receiver that gets one MUST reply with its own. A receiver MAY close an idle connection, and MUST attempt a close_notify exchange first. Alerts are not retransmitted and may be lost.
sections.plainLanguage: Each note starts with a number saying how long it is, so the reader knows where one note stops and the next starts. When finished, you say goodbye, and the other side says goodbye back.

sections.title: Congestion Control and Security Policy
sections.content:
Syslog can generate unlimited data, and UDP has no congestion control, which makes sending it over UDP generally problematic. DCCP has congestion control, so syslog over DTLS over DCCP is RECOMMENDED in preference to UDP where DCCP is available. DCCP implementations MUST support CCID 3 and SHOULD support CCID 2. The congestion considerations of RFC 5426 also apply over UDP.

The security policies are meant to match syslog over TLS, and all the normative requirements of Section 5 of RFC 5425 apply.
sections.plainLanguage: Sending without slowing down can clog the mail truck. One kind of road has traffic lights that make senders slow down, so it is preferred.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The considerations of RFC 4347, RFC 5246, RFC 5425 and RFC 5280 apply. The RFC adds four points.

  • Renegotiation: it is RECOMMENDED to disable it. If allowed, RFC 5746 MUST be followed and identities in certificates MUST NOT change.
  • Message loss: the transports are unreliable, and an attacker may remove messages unnoticed. Those wanting a lossless stream should use TLS over TCP, and signed syslog (RFC 5848) can indicate loss.
  • Key generation: a weak random number generator can leave little or no security; see RFC 4086.
  • Trust anchors: installation and storage are critical and need out-of-band steps. The certificate fingerprint can confirm that a self-signed certificate was installed correctly.
sections.plainLanguage: Locks only help if the keys are made well and kept safe. Also, this mail service can lose letters, and nobody may notice.
